description_full: Columbia Sportswear Company, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the design, development, marketing, and distribution of outdoor, active, and lifestyle products in the United States, Latin America, the Asia Pacific, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Canada. It provides apparel, accessories, and equipment for hiking, trail running, snow, fishing, hunting, and outdoor activities. The company also offers footwear products that include hiking boots; trail running shoes; rugged cold weather boots; sandals and shoes for use in water activities; and footwear for lifestyle wear. It serves its products through wholesale distribution channel comprising small independently operated specialty outdoor and sporting goods stores, sporting goods chains, department store chains, internet retailers, and international distributors, as well as through direct-to-consumer distribution channel, including a network of branded, outlet, temporary clearance and employee retail stores, brand-specific e-commerce sites, and shop-in-shop retail locations. It sells its products under the Columbia, Mountain Hardwear, PRANA, and SOREL brands. Columbia Sportswear Company was founded in 1938 and is headquartered in Portland, Oregon.

financial_summary: Columbia Sportswear Company is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $3.8B market cap on $3.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 49%.

The business throws off $217M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.60× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 7.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 59% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 24% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.

val: The stock trades only 9% below its DCF fair value of $82.30, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 59%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $65.60 to $107 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.7% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.2% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 9.0% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.42).
It runs a 49% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.60x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $790.8M (21% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.6% over 3 years, 6.3% over 5 years and 3.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -2.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 1.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 98.0% on average.
own: Insiders own 58.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 54%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $2.7M sold).
It returns 7.1% a year to shareholders (5.3% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 19 consecutive years, raising it 5.2% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 19.0% of the float, 6.2 days to cover.
people: With about 9,620 employees, each generates about $353K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 5.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $23K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.0M (9x revenue per employee).
